reconcile.connective: Gill reads "the twelve" as the apostles' retained title of office, not a literal headcount, though he flags that some ancient witnesses read "the eleven" instead.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the count directly, suggesting Paul may simply not have known the Judas-betrayal tradition when he wrote "the twelve."

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: "How Can Paul Say that Jesus Appeared to the Twelve?" (The Bart Ehrman Blog)
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, "How Can Paul Say that Jesus Appeared to the Twelve?", The Bart Ehrman Blog (April 12, 2022)

excerpts.excerpt_text: then of the twelve; though there were then but eleven of them, Judas being gone from them, and having destroyed himself; and at the first appearance of Christ to them, there were but ten present, Thomas being absent; and yet because their original number, when first chosen and called, were twelve, they still went by the same name … The Vulgate Latin reads the "eleven"; and so the Claromontane exemplar.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill explicitly concedes the resurrection-appearance group numbered only eleven at that moment (Judas already dead) and explains the KJV's 'twelve' as the apostles' retained original-number title, while also noting the Vulgate/Claromontane manuscripts read 'the eleven' — directly on this row's numerical tension.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on 1 Corinthians 15:5
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Haley's Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible does not treat this specific tension (confirmed by a full-text search of the djvu text and its scripture index, which lists only 'Apostles, lists of names' and 'called when' entries); Gill's own note on 1 Corinthians 15:5, already surfaced on this row, treats the eleven-vs-twelve headcount directly and flags the Vulgate/Claromontane 'eleven' reading.
